rashi:a1.1: And here they found another verse and expounded it: that if he consecrated it and afterward his father died, it is an ancestral field. For otherwise, if the verse included for us only [the case where] his father died and afterward he consecrated it, let the verse write “which is not his ancestral field,” and Rabbi Meir’s [ruling] would be included [by it], since he expounds: excluding this one, which is already an ancestral field.
rashi:a1.2: Why do I need “of the field”? Conclude from it what we said: to expound [the case where] he consecrated it and afterward his father died.
rashi:a1.3: Excluding this one: which at the time of consecration was due to become an ancestral field.
rashi:a2.1: Even an Israelite too: for it is taught at the beginning of our chapter (Arakhin 24a): one may consecrate before the Jubilee, and so on. (And if it is because our mishna teaches that one may not consecrate less than two years before the Jubilee, we established there that it teaches us good advice.)
rashi:a3.1: This works out well according to Shmuel, who says: with an Israelite it is not consecrated; [so] it was necessary to teach us that with priests it is consecrated.
rashi:a3.2: But according to Rav: one cannot say this, for from where in the verses would we come to it?
rashi:a4.1: Since he taught in the first clause: [the case] of an Israelite, he taught in the latter clause [the case] of Levites.
rashi:a7.1: Mishna. One who consecrates his field at a time when there is no Jubilee: at a time when the Jubilee is not in effect.
rashi:a7.2: You open first: for how much do you want to redeem it? For the sake of the Temple’s profit, they ask him first.
rashi:a7.3: As the owners give a fifth: and that is why it specified “at a time when the Jubilee is not in effect.” For at a time when it is in effect there is no need to ask him for how much he will redeem it, since its price is fixed: a beit kor for fifty sela. And it is speaking of an ancestral field; and at a time when the Jubilee is not in effect, it is redeemed at its value, as it is taught at the end of our chapter: [the law of] an ancestral field applies only at a time when the Jubilee is in effect.
tosafot:a7.1: Mishna. One who consecrates his field at a time when the Jubilee is not in effect: meaning, at a time when the Jubilee is not in effect, for then it is redeemed at its value, and there is profit for the Temple in having the owners open first, because of the fifth. But at a time when the Jubilee is in effect it is redeemed according to its seed: fifty sela for the area sown with a ḥomer of barley. And it speaks of an ancestral field, and of the time of the Temple, when there is profit for the Temple. For if not in the time of the Temple, one may desacralize it, if he wishes, even ab initio, onto the equivalent of a peruta, since there is no profit in it for the Temple, as it goes to waste; as is found below at the end of our chapter (Arakhin 29a): a certain man who devoted his property came before Rav Yehuda; he said to him: Take four zuz, desacralize [the property] onto them, throw them into the river, and it will be permitted to you. And if you ask: how can there be a time with no Jubilee in the time of the Temple? One can say: at the time when [some of] Israel were exiled, for we require “all its inhabitants upon it.”
gershom:a5.1: He says to him: to the one who consecrated, when they announce it for redemption, [he says to the owners]: You open first; for how much do you want to redeem it? For if no one is found who wants to redeem it for more than the owners, it is better that the owners redeem it, for the Temple’s profit, since the owners add a fifth onto their redemption.
rashi:a8.1: Due to its inferior quality: its expenses were greater than its yield.
gershom:a6.1: Due to its inferior quality: either because its tax was great, or because the expense was greater than the yield.
gershom:a7.1: And they said to him: You open first; and he said: It is hereby mine for an issar: for he did not think it worth more, because of its poor quality.
rashi:a8.2: He did not say “for an issar”; rather: “It is hereby mine for an egg,” for consecrated property is redeemed with money and with the equivalent of money.
tosafot:a8.1: Rabbi Yosei said, and so on: It is puzzling: how could this incident have taken place in the days of Rabbi Yosei? Rabbi Yosei did not live in the time of the Temple, and if so, there was no need to open first with the owners. One can say that he disagrees on the basis of a tradition [he received] that it happened in the time of the Temple. Alternatively, even not in the time of the Temple, redemption is first with the owners, as it is written (Leviticus 27:27): “And if it is not redeemed, then it shall be sold.”
gershom:a8.1: Rabbi Yosei said: the incident was not so. That is, he did not say “It is hereby mine for an issar” but “It is hereby mine for an egg.” And from here you learn that consecrated property is not like second tithe, which is redeemed only with money; rather, consecrated property is redeemed with money and with the equivalent of money.
rashi:a8.3: He said to him: the treasurer [said to him].
rashi:a8.4: It has come to you: it is hereby yours.
gershom:a9.1: They said to him: It has come to you: let it be yours, and give the issar.
gershom:a10.1: He loses an issar: which he gives to the Temple.
gershom:a11.1: And his field is before him: it is his, with its poor quality, and he has two losses after the return: one, that his field returned to him; and one, that he lost the issar.
rashi:a9.1: Gemara. But isn’t it taught: they force: the owners to open first.
gershom:a12.1: But isn’t it taught: they force: for the sake of the Temple’s profit [the text in parentheses reads “because he consecrated it”], so that he will add a fifth.
tosafot:a9.1: What is “says”? They force: And if you ask: why is coercion needed here more than in all those that we learned at the end of the first chapter of Bekhorot (13a): the mitzva of redemption takes precedence over the mitzva of breaking the neck; the mitzva of designation takes precedence over the mitzva of redemption; the mitzva of levirate marriage takes precedence over the mitzva of ḥalitza; the mitzva of redemption by the owner takes precedence over anyone else? It derives all of them there from verses, and we do not find coercion except in this one. One can say that here is different, because it can lead to a stumbling block if people derive benefit from it.
rashi:a10.1: That the mitzva of redemption is with the owner: in the first chapter of Bekhorot (13a).
gershom:a13.1: That since it is dear to him he would increase and redeem it: that is, since he knows better than another how much it yields, he will add to its redemption more than one who does not know it.
gershom:a14.1: And furthermore, the mitzva of redemption is with the owner: as we learned in the first chapter of Bekhorot: the mitzva of redemption by the owner takes precedence over anyone else.
rashi:a11.1: He would increase and redeem it: he adds and redeems it for more than other people.
rashi:a11.2: The mitzva of redemption is with the owner: as it is written (Leviticus 27:27): “And if it is not redeemed, then it shall be sold according to your valuation”; evidently the mitzva of redemption takes precedence over sale.
rashi:a13.1: But don’t we maintain that the equivalent of money is like money: as we say in Bava Kamma (7a): “He shall return” — to include the equivalent of money, even bran.
gershom:a15.1: He states one and another, and so on. And don’t we maintain everywhere that the equivalent of money is like money, except for second tithe?
tosafot:a13.1: Rabbi Yosei holds one may redeem even with something like an egg: In the chapter HaZahav (Bava Metzia 53b) there is a dispute: one opinion says [it must be worth a peruta] in itself and in its fifth, and one says in itself, even though not in its fifth. And it seems that “like an egg” means the equivalent of a peruta.
gershom:a16.1: One may redeem even with something like an egg: even though its fifth is not worth a peruta.
rashi:a14.1: This unspecified [statement]: which teaches “he loses an issar” and does not teach “he is found to lose an egg,” is the Rabbis and not Rabbi Yosei.
gershom:a17.1: The unspecified ruling accords with the Rabbis, who say its fifth must be worth a peruta [that is, the first tanna, not Rabbi Yosei, who said “It is hereby mine for an issar”; and we learn from it that one does not redeem with something whose fifth is not worth a peruta].
gershom:a18.1: And one said for fifty: like the Torah’s valuation, as it is written: “fifty shekels of silver.”
gershom:a19.1: The one of fifty reneged: that he regretted it.
gershom:a20.1: One repossesses from his property up to ten: that is, one takes collateral from him to the measure of the addition that he added beyond the others, since his statement to the Most High is like his delivery to an ordinary person. And likewise all of them: when they renege, one takes collateral from each to the measure of what he added over his fellow.
rashi:a15.1: Mishna. One repossesses from his property ten sela: it turns out that the treasurer has twenty in hand [after the bidders of fifty and forty reneged], and so [the bidder of] thirty gives thirty; that makes fifty.
gershom:a21.1: If the one of ten reneged, one sells it at its value; and if they could not sell it [for ten], one collects the remainder from the one of ten until the Temple has ten sela from it, since he assessed it at ten sela.
rashi:a17.1: One said: It is hereby mine for twenty-one: after the owners said twenty.
rashi:b1.1: The owners give: against their will.
rashi:b1.2: Twenty-six: for we do not give it to this one, since the owners said twenty and the reckoning with the fifth comes to twenty-five; and if [the treasurer] gave it to that one for twenty-one, the Temple would be found to lose. So the owners give, against their will, that sela which this one added to the principal, and their own twenty-five; but on the sela that this one added they do not add a fifth.
gershom:b12.1: One said: It is hereby mine for twenty-one sela; the owners give twenty-six. For the owners said twenty and add a further fifth on the twenty, making twenty-six [with the other’s added sela]. And so always they force the owners to redeem it themselves, because they add a fifth, and they also give the addition that the other added over twenty. But the owners do not add a fifth on the increase that the other raises over twenty; rather, they give the addition alone on top of their own fifth. For example, if one said “It is hereby mine for twenty-five,” the owners give thirty and no more: five for their fifth and five for this one’s addition. But if one said “It is hereby mine for twenty-six,” they do not force the owners to redeem it, as we say in the Gemara, for they can say “A man has come in our place [baḥarikin],” who added on the twenty the equivalent of the fifth that we were obligated to add; from now on we are not obligated to redeem, unless the owners still wish to redeem it.
rashi:b2.1: One said twenty-five; the owners give thirty: against their will. And now one could object: why do they force the owners? Granted, until now we force them, since we cannot give it to these others, because their principal is not as much as the principal and fifth that the owners said first; therefore we perforce return to the owners, and since we return to the owners they must give the principal as the others assessed it, and their own fifth. But now that one said twenty-five, let them give it to that one, for his principal equals the principal and fifth that the owners said first. And in the Gemara it raises this objection.
gershom:b13.1: If they wished to give thirty-one and a dinar: for so the reckoning comes to, between their fifth and this one’s addition; the owners take precedence.
gershom:b14.1: And if not: that the owners did not wish to give so much.
gershom:b15.1: He says to him: to this one who said twenty-six.
gershom:b16.1: It has come to you: give what you said, and it is yours.
rashi:b4.1: Gemara. They taught only: that one repossesses from the property of the bidder of fifty only ten sela, when the bidder of forty stands in his place and does not renege. But if the bidder of forty reneged, they divide the twenty sela [lost] between fifty and thirty between them: the bidder of fifty gives fifteen and the bidder of forty gives five. For in the ten that the bidder of fifty said beyond the bidder of forty, the bidder of forty has no share in the loss with him; but the ten that the bidder of forty added over the bidder of thirty, the bidder of fifty also agreed to, along with the forty, since forty is included in fifty.
gershom:b1.1: They taught only: that when the one of fifty reneged, one repossesses from his property up to ten and no more, only when the bidder of forty stands in his place, so that they do not divide between them, since now the Temple has been reduced by ten shekels.
gershom:b2.1: They divide this reduction between them: the bidder of fifty gives fifteen shekels and the bidder of forty gives five shekels.
gershom:b3.1: What is the reason? This bidder of fifty gives the ten that he added by himself, without dispute. And as for the ten shekels that the bidder of forty added over the bidder of thirty, the bidder of forty says to the bidder of fifty: You too share with me in my ten, since these forty are included in fifty. Therefore he gives half of these ten as well. And the other ten shekels he gives alone, since there is no other bidder of fifty, for no one else assessed it at fifty.
rashi:b6.1: Where there is no bidder of fifty: that no one said more than forty, for the mishna teaches case by case.
gershom:b4.1: Let the bidder of forty give fifteen, so that he is drawn in for half of these ten of the bidder of thirty.
gershom:b5.1: If there is a bidder of forty, so indeed; but [this is] where there is no bidder of forty; therefore the bidder of thirty gives ten.
gershom:b6.1: If so: as Rav Ḥisda said.
gershom:b7.1: Say the latter clause: the one of ten reneged, and so on.
rashi:b8.1: Let the bidder of twenty give with him: for he too agreed to ten.
rashi:b8.2: From the one of ten: since it teaches “from the one of ten,” this implies that there is another.
gershom:b8.1: If so: if there is only [the bidder of] ten [alone], why did it need to say “one collects from the one of ten”? It should have said “one collects from him.” Rather, since it teaches “one collects from the one of ten,” conclude from it that there is also a bidder of twenty, and it does not teach that they divide between them; and it is difficult for Rav Ḥisda.
gershom:b9.1: Rather, it is not difficult: here, where all of them reneged at once, they divide [between them]; but where they reneged one after another, one collects from each his own addition.
rashi:b9.1: If they reneged all at once they divide between them: as Rav Ḥisda [said]; and the mishna is where they reneged one after another, for then the bidder of fifty says to the treasurer: When I reneged, I left you the bidder of forty.
rashi:b9.2: They divide between them: the first ones gain and the last two lose [the printed text reads “two and three first ones gain and two last ones lose”: compared with reneging one after another, those who bid first (10, 20, 30) pay less and the last two (40, 50) pay more]. For if all of them reneged and the treasurer sold it at its value, [say] five sela, there is a shortfall of forty-five sela. The bidder of fifty gives the ten that are his alone. Of the ten of the bidder of forty, he gives half, for both of them agreed to them. Of the ten of the bidder of thirty, the bidder of fifty gives a third, the bidder of forty a third and the bidder of thirty a third, for all three of them said thirty. The ten of the bidder of twenty, all four of them give between them. And the five by which [the sale] fell short of the bidder of ten, all five of them give.
gershom:b10.1: This is also taught: that when all reneged together they divide between them. How? The one of fifty gives fifteen; the one of forty gives five of his addition and five [of the addition] of the bidder of thirty; the bidder of thirty gives half his addition [and half of the addition of the bidder of twenty; and the bidder of twenty gives half his addition] and half of the remainder that is collected from the bidder of ten.
gershom:b11.1: But didn’t we learn: one repossesses from the property of each one up to ten? Rather, must one not conclude from it as Rav Ḥisda, as we resolved: here at once, there one after another?
rashi:b10.1: Some raise them as a contradiction: and they do not teach this [statement] of Rav Ḥisda on its own, but only by way of resolving the mishna and the baraita that contradict each other.
tosafot:b11.1: Is this to say that the fifth is preferable? And raise a contradiction: the householder says: for a sela: Rabbi Elḥanan found it puzzling: what is the objection? One cannot object from [the clause] “the owners say twenty and anyone says twenty, the owners take precedence,” while here it is taught that the other takes precedence — what difficulty is that? For the owners take precedence only when no other redeems it for more. Nor can one object from the latter clause, where it is taught: one said “It is hereby mine for twenty-one,” the owners take precedence and give twenty-six, while here it is taught that the other takes precedence. That too is not difficult: for the reason [there] is only that he adds to the principal, which is twenty; so too in our mishna it is right that the owners take precedence, since they too add to the principal when they give twenty-six, for they give the one beyond the twenty, and the fifth on account of the principal, [so that the principal] is twenty-one. Perhaps, then, he objects thus: why is it different here, that the owners are forced to give the sum the other said, and the fifth on what [the owner] himself said, as it teaches “the owners give twenty-six, twenty-seven”; whereas there it is taught that when the householder says “for a sela” and the other says “for a sela and an issar,” [the one of a sela and an issar] takes precedence, and we do not force the householder to give a sela and an issar with the fifth? For it teaches “the one of a sela and an issar takes precedence,” and does not teach “the householder gives five dinars,” which is principal and fifth, and an issar. And it answers: here, the fifth is the Temple’s gain, so the fifth is preferable, and therefore we force the owners; there, the fifth is the householder’s gain, and so on.
rashi:b11.1: [The householder says: for a sela:] A householder who redeems his own second tithe adds a fifth, as it is written (Leviticus 27:31): “And if a man will redeem any of his tithe,” and so on; and another who redeems it does not add a fifth. The householder says “for a sela” and another says “for a sela and an issar,” and so on: [the latter takes precedence] because he adds to the principal, even though the householder would have to give more, since a fifth of a sela is a dinar, and a dinar is twenty-four issarin, [as stated] in the first chapter of Kiddushin (12a).
gershom:b17.1: And the householder says: to redeem his second tithe for a sela, and another says: Give it to me and I will give a sela and an issar for it. The one of a sela and an issar takes precedence over the householder, and the tithe will be his, because he adds an issar to the principal beyond the householder. And even though, when the householder redeems it, he is obligated to add a fifth, as it is written: “And if a man will redeem any of his tithe, he shall add to it the fifth part thereof,” and another does not add a fifth, even so the one of a sela and an issar takes precedence over the householder.
gershom:b18.1: And it answers: it is not difficult. For here, with one who redeems his field, the fifth that the owners add is the Temple’s gain, since principal and fifth come into the treasurer’s hand; therefore the one who gives a fifth to the Temple is preferable.
rashi:b12.1: There: with regard to second tithe, the fifth is the householder’s gain, for both principal and fifth are all his, and he will eat it all in Jerusalem. We have in it only the mitzva of redemption, that he not eat it in the outlying areas without redemption, and the essence of its redemption is with the principal. And even though the money is less, we do not care, since only he benefits from the extra money.
gershom:b19.1: Here [there]: with second tithe, the fifth he adds is the householder’s gain, for the principal and fifth belong to the householder, and he brings it up and eats it in Jerusalem as tithe; and when he adds a fifth, this is his gain, that he has more money with which to buy all his needs in Jerusalem. Therefore the one who redeems the principal properly, adding an issar more than the householder in its redemption, takes precedence over the householder, even though the householder adds a fifth. Since neither the principal nor the fifth comes into the Temple’s hand, but into the householder’s hand, we do not care about that fifth; rather, the one who redeems the principal better than his fellow takes precedence.
rashi:b13.1: And let the owners say: A man has come in our place [baḥarikin]: who wants to give as much as we. Granted, until now you came back to us because of the Temple’s loss; but now, why do you want to force us?
gershom:b20.1: And why do the owners give thirty? Let the owners say: A man has already come in our place [baḥarikin], who wants to give as much as our principal and fifth, and from now on we are exempt.
rashi:b13.2: Where the owners said: at the outset, a dinar more than twenty, so that the reckoning of principal and fifth reaches twenty-five and a dinar; and if we gave it to this one, the Temple would lose. Therefore we return to the owners against their will.
gershom:b21.1: No: they cannot say this, as where the owners said twenty and a dinar, they are obligated to give twenty-five and a dinar, and this man said only twenty-five; therefore one cannot say “A man has come in our place.”
rashi:b14.1: And let it teach: in the first clause of the mishna: the owners say twenty and a dinar.
gershom:b22.1: If so, why does it not teach “the owners say twenty and a dinar”? Let it teach a dinar.
rashi:b14.2: It is not meticulous: to teach a dinar, only the reckoning of sela’im.
gershom:b23.1: It is not meticulous: the tanna did not want to teach a dinar, which is less than a shekel.
rashi:b14.3: But it teaches: a dinar in the latter clause; evidently it is meticulous about dinars.
gershom:b24.1: And is it not [meticulous]? But it teaches a dinar in the latter clause!
rashi:b14.4: Rather, Rava said: where the owners said at the outset [twenty and] a peruta; and about perutot it is not meticulous.
gershom:b25.1: Rather, Rava said: where the owners said twenty and a peruta, they are obligated to give twenty-five and a peruta, and the other man said only twenty-five alone, and he cannot say “A man has come in our place.” And since the owners said a peruta, and a peruta is not a significant thing, the tanna did not want to teach it.
rashi:b15.1: That the consecrated property was not appraised by three: that three people did not appraise the land at what this other one said.
gershom:b26.1: They taught only: that one does not add a fifth on this one’s increase only when the consecrated property was not appraised by three people.
rashi:b15.2: But: if three appraised it according to this one’s words, the owners add a fifth on his increase against their will, and we do not require ten. And even though the appraisal of consecrated property requires ten, as we say in Sanhedrin (2a): land, nine and a priest, here it teaches us a novelty: since three said so, we do not go back to [look for] ten, and they add a fifth on the increase.
gershom:b27.1: But: if that other one appraised it with the judgment of three people, that it is worth such and such above twenty, the owners also add a fifth even on that increase.
tosafot:b16.1: It is taught: Beit Shammai say they add: This is how we read it, and so it is written in the book of Rabbeinu Tam; and we do not read “this is also taught.” And if we do read it, it can be explained thus: “this is also taught,” that there is one who holds that they add [the fifth] when it was appraised, whether according to Beit Shammai or according to Beit Hillel, and the Gemara is exacting to find [this] in accordance with Rav Ḥisda. But it seems more likely that one reads “it is taught,” without “also.”
gershom:b28.1: This is also taught, and so on.
gershom:b29.1: Actually, where it was not appraised; but where it was appraised, even Beit Hillel agree that they add. And as for what is difficult for you: what is the reason of Beit Shammai, who say they add?
gershom:b30.1: Beit Shammai are stringent: they say so merely as a stringency. And if you wish, say: where it was appraised, and reverse [the opinions]; and Rav Ḥisda is like Beit Hillel, who [then] say they add.
rashi:b18.1: Six matters are among the leniencies of Beit Shammai and the stringencies of Beit Hillel.
gershom:b31.1: If so, that Beit Hillel are stringent in saying they add a fifth on the increase, let it be taught among the leniencies of Beit Shammai and the stringencies of Beit Hillel. Rather, actually, as we said at first: where it was not appraised [and even so Beit Shammai are stringent in saying they add]; but where it was appraised, even Beit Hillel hold that they add; and Rav Ḥisda speaks as Beit Hillel.
gershom:b32.1: If they wished, yes; if they did not wish, no: [for one does not force them]. What is the reason? For they can say: A man has come in our place.
rashi:b21.1: And the dinar, what is its purpose? But you said that one does not add a fifth on this one’s increase!
gershom:b33.1: That dinar, what is its purpose? [It has already been taught] that one does not add a fifth on this one’s increase, and this dinar looks like a fifth of that sixth [sela] above twenty.
rashi:b21.2: At the outset: when they opened first.
rashi:b21.3: To give a reckoning that reaches: beyond this one’s increase, to thirty-one and a dinar.
gershom:b34.1: Rav Sheshet said this is what it is saying: since the owners said “It is hereby mine for twenty-one” before this one spoke, and now they must give, between principal and fifth, twenty-six shekels and a dinar; if they wish to give so, the owners take precedence.
gershom:a1.1: They found and expounded: that this one, which is due to become an ancestral field, is excluded; and not for the reason that acquisition of the produce is not like acquisition of the body.
gershom:a2.1: That it teaches us that priests and Levites redeem always: even in the Jubilee Year.
gershom:a3.1: Rav would say to you: And according to your reasoning, since he may consecrate in the Jubilee Year itself, conclude [that he may] both before the Jubilee and after the Jubilee; so why do I need to teach it? Rather, since he taught in the first clause of the mishna: one may not consecrate before the Jubilee, and may not redeem after the Jubilee, less than a year, he also taught in the latter clause: both before the Jubilee, and so on. And since he taught “one may not consecrate [and may not redeem],” he also taught in the latter clause “they consecrate and redeem.” And in truth, “they consecrate always” did not need to be taught; only “they redeem” was needed, as stated; and since he taught “they redeem always,” he taught “they consecrate always.”
